entry.title: AI as a layer of abstraction
entry.summary: Language models are the newest layer between us and the machine. Like every layer before them, they leak; what matters is whether you can see it.
entry.content:
Every generation of tools has moved us one layer further from the machine. Assemblers spared us opcodes, compilers spared us registers, and frameworks spared us the plumbing. Language models feel like the next layer, and like every layer before them, they leak.

What a good layer does#

A good abstraction lets you forget the layer below most of the time, and tells you clearly when you cannot. The trouble with a model as a layer is the second half: when it is wrong, it is wrong fluently.

The useful question is not whether the layer leaks, but whether you can see the leak.

How I use it#

  • For code I could write myself, faster.

  • For a first draft I will rewrite, never a final one.

  • Never for a decision I cannot check.

There is a longer version of this argument in my reading notes, which are not published yet.

entry.title: Why Your Jetson Won't Stay Bricked (Probably)
entry.summary: A bad flash feels final. It almost never is: the boot ROM keeps a recovery path that no update can overwrite.
entry.content:
The first time a Jetson refuses to boot after a bad flash, it feels final. It almost never is. The board keeps a recovery path in its boot ROM that no update can overwrite.

Recovery mode#

  1. Power the board off.

  2. Hold the recovery button and power it on.

  3. Connect it to a Linux host over USB.

lsusb | grep -i nvidia
sudo ./flash.sh jetson-orin-nano-devkit internal

Warning

Flash from a host running the exact JetPack release you are installing. Mixing versions is the usual cause of a second brick.

The boot chain, briefly#

Diagram source
flowchart LR
  ROM --> MB1 --> MB2 --> UEFI --> Kernel

Once you know the chain, a failure stops being mysterious: the serial console tells you which stage stopped.

entry.title: The admin panel has no password
entry.summary: Most home networks hold one device whose settings page opens with no login at all. Here is why, and how to find yours.
entry.content:
Scan a home network and you will find at least one device whose web admin page opens straight to the settings. No login, no warning. It is usually something nobody remembers installing.

Why it keeps happening#

Devices ship with the panel open so setup is easy, and the step that closes it is optional. Optional security steps are skipped steps.

What to do on your own network#

  • List every device that answers on port 80 or 443

  • Set a password on each admin page

  • Move devices onto their own network segment

entry.title: Kubernetes made my life easier
entry.summary: I resisted Kubernetes for my side projects for years. Too much machinery for three services. Then I ran three services by hand for a year. Restarts...
entry.content:
I resisted Kubernetes for my side projects for years. Too much machinery for three services. Then I ran three services by hand for a year.

What changed#

  • Restarts, rollouts and health checks stopped being scripts I maintained.

  • Every service declares what it needs in one place.

  • Moving to a new machine became a matter of pointing the cluster at it.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobbie-api
spec:
  replicas: 2

It is still too much for a single static site. It is about right for anything with a database and a worker.
